bipartite.note: The translator did not attempt any actual translation of the poem's content; instead he provided a note declaring the poem untranslatable due to its wordplay, deferring explanation to an appendix. No bipartite structure of kami/shimo is rendered at all, so the relationship is effectively collapsed into non-existence in the translation proper.

kakekotoba_handling.note: No English rendering of the reed-cutting/temporary-sleeping pun is given; the translator explicitly states the poem's wordplay defeats translation.
The one-night/reed-joint pun is entirely absent from the translation text, which contains no rendering of the poem at all.
The exhausting-oneself/channel-marker pun is likewise not rendered; the translator only remarks on the poem's untranslatability.

kigo_handling.note: No seasonal imagery of reeds or autumn marshland appears anywhere in the translation text, which consists solely of a meta-commentary about the poem's puns being impossible to render.

entries.content_summary: A translator's note explaining that the poem's puns (plays upon words) make it untranslatable with the force of the original, and referring the reader to an appendix for explanation.

line_mapping.structural_note: There is no actual translation of any ku; the single 'line' is entirely a meta-textual disclaimer rather than a rendering of source content, so no kami/shimo mapping is possible.

Dickens.translator_strategy: Rather than attempting a translation, Dickens opts to flag the poem's untranslatable wordplay directly to the reader and relegate any interpretive content to a separate appendix, prioritizing honesty about linguistic limits over producing an English poem.

bipartite.note: The translator retains the simile structure explicitly with 'Like a joint of the shore reed' but compresses the shimo-ku into a single short question line, losing the sustained homophonic bridge (身をつくし/澪標) that ties Naniwa setting to the emotional register; the simile is stated overtly rather than implied through the pivot word, so the rhetorical mechanism is replaced by an explicit comparison.

kakekotoba_handling.note: The translator collapses the reed-cutting image and the brief-sleep image into a generic phrase 'short one night love' without conveying either the physical cut-reed-stubble image or the temporary-sleep nuance distinctly; the pivot's double meaning is dissolved into paraphrase.

The 'one night' reading survives as the literal number of nights, but the secondary reading as a reed-joint/segment is instead relocated into a separate explicit simile ('Like a joint of the shore reed'), so the pivot's fusion is split apart rather than held together in one word.

Only the 'exhausting/wearing out one's body' meaning survives; the channel-marker stake (澪標) image and its link back to the Naniwa bay setting is entirely lost, so the associative link connecting shimo back to kami is severed.

kigo_handling.note: The word 'reed' survives as a bare noun and evokes waterside vegetation, but without the cutting/withering action (かりね) rendered concretely, the autumnal desolation and transience specifically associated with cut reed-stubble is diminished to a generic simile object rather than a seasonal marker.

entries.content_summary: States the brevity of the one-night love directly, moving the 一夜 concept to the opening line
Locates the scene at Naniwa shore, echoing kami-ku's setting
Explicit simile comparing the night's brevity to a reed joint, fusing the かりね image and the 一夜/節 pivot into one stated comparison
Compresses the shimo-ku's rhetorical question about exhausting longing into a short direct question

line_mapping.structural_note: The translator front-loads the 'one night' concept (normally ku3) into line 1, then returns to the setting (ku1) in line 2, and states the かりね/一夜 pivot as an explicit simile in line 3 — an inversion of ku order for rhetorical clarity — before compressing all of shimo-ku (ku4+ku5) into a single terse final line.

Noguchi.translator_strategy: Noguchi prioritizes clarity and brevity over preserving the pivot-word mechanics, converting the kakekotoba's implicit double meanings into an explicit, stated simile and losing the imagery web that ties the Naniwa landscape to the speaker's emotional exhaustion.

bipartite.note: Porter keeps the kami-no-ku as an explicit simile ('as short... as bamboo reeds') rather than the source's implicit pivot-based simile, and the shimo-no-ku is compressed into a rhetorical question about measuring love against tide-stakes; the logical connective survives (brevity of encounter vs. depth/measure of love) but the mechanism is made explicit rather than implicit, and the 身をつくして self-exhausting motif is replaced by a 'gauge' metaphor, weakening the original's fusion of landscape and passion into a more generic comparison.

kakekotoba_handling.note: Porter keeps the physical reed image ('bamboo reeds at Naniwa') but drops the 仮寝 (brief sleeping/tryst) secondary meaning entirely; the reeds are used only as a simile for shortness of time, not as a pun on temporary lodging.
The 'one night' sense is rendered as 'a few short hours', preserving the primary temporal meaning but losing any trace of the reed-joint (節) secondary pun.

Porter converts the channel-marker stakes (澪標) into 'tide-stakes' used as a measuring device metaphor ('Can't gauge my love'), abandoning the literal self-exhaustion sense (身を尽くし) altogether and inventing a new rhetorical function (an inadequate measuring instrument) rather than preserving either original reading.

kigo_handling.note: The reeds survive as an image ('bamboo reeds at Naniwa') giving a faint waterside/marsh atmosphere, but there is no cutting, withering, or stubble imagery, so the autumnal desolation of かりね is lost; only a generic reed-bed picture remains.

entries.content_summary: The brevity of the encounter stated directly ('a few short hours')
Comparative clause setting up the simile ('As short, they seemed to me')
The reed image at Naniwa used as the vehicle of comparison ('bamboo reeds at Naniwa')
Introduces tide-stakes (澪標) as a measuring device
Declares that even tide-stakes cannot measure the speaker's love, replacing the original's self-exhausting longing with an inadequacy-of-measurement conceit

line_mapping.structural_note: Porter inverts the sequence, opening with the shimo-no-ku's emotional claim (brevity of time together) before introducing the kami-no-ku's reed simile, then closes with an extrapolated 'gauge' conceit built from 澪標 that has no direct equivalent in the source's plain declarative structure.

Porter.translator_strategy: Porter prioritizes a smooth, rhyme-driven English quatrain-like structure over preserving the puns, converting the reed and channel-marker wordplay into two explicit similes (short time = short reeds; love = immeasurable by tide-stakes) at the cost of the original's implicit image network and double meanings.

bipartite.note: McCauley preserves the basic kami/shimo division and even makes the simile between the brief reed-node and the one night explicit ('Short as is a node of reed') rather than leaving it implicit as in the source. This is a partial preservation: the relationship type is maintained (comparison between reed-segment and brief night) but the rhetorical subtlety of pivot-word driven implicit simile is flattened into an explicit simile stated in English syntax.

kakekotoba.note: McCauley drops the 'kariné' (cut stubble / temporary sleeping) pivot entirely, replacing it with 'node of reed,' which shifts to the 一夜 reed-joint imagery instead; the transient-sleep meaning and the cut-stubble literal image are both lost.

The 'one night' meaning is rendered literally and clearly, but the secondary reed-joint (ひとよ=節) pun is instead attached to 'node of reed' as a separate simile rather than fused into the same word, so the pivot's double-duty is separated into two phrases rather than preserved as a single word.

McCauley renders only the emotional 'exhausting oneself/whole heart' sense; the channel-marker (澪標) image and its tie to the Naniwa bay setting is entirely dropped, so the wordplay linking landscape to passion is lost.

kigo.note: The reed imagery survives ('node of reed... Grown in Naniwa bay') giving a marshland/waterside atmosphere, but there is no cutting or withering imagery (no 'kariné' stubble), so the autumnal desolation connoted by cut reeds is softened into a more neutral botanical image of a reed's node; the season is not named and its withering connotation is weakened though the waterside reed setting remains.

entries.content_summary: For the sake of just one night
as short as a single node/joint of reed
grown in Naniwa bay (the reed's setting)
must I henceforth long for him
with my whole heart / exhausting myself, until life's end

line_mapping.structural_note: McCauley reorders the kami-no-ku material: he leads with the 'one night' concept (ku3) before the reed/bay imagery (ku1-2), effectively inverting the internal sequence of the kami-no-ku while keeping the kami/shimo macro-division intact; he also adds 'till life's close' as an interpretive expansion not literally present in the source but consonant with 身を尽くして's exhaustion sense.

McCauley.translator_strategy: McCauley favors clarity and explicit simile over preserving the compressed double-meanings of the original, sacrificing the kakekotoba's wordplay to produce a smoothly readable English quatrain-like statement of longing.
